newsitem.title: EGYPT: Syria says unshaken by Israel gas warning.
newsitem.headline: Syria says unshaken by Israel gas warning.

text.p: President Hafez al-Assad said on Thursday Syria was not shaken by a warning from Israel over a more lethal nerve gas that the Jewish state says Damascus is making.
"We heard the threats but they did not create an earthquake in Syria. Neither threats nor any thing else will shake Syria," Assad said.
He was addressing a news conference in the southern Sinai resort of Sharm el-Sheikh after four hours of talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
Israel said on Tuesday Syria was making a more lethal nerve gas and warned Damascus the Jewish state had means many times more destructive at its proposal.

"He who has nuclear weapons has no right to criticise others for whatever weapons they have. If they (Israel) want disarmament let's start with nuclear weapons. Arabs in general are ready to get rid of other weapons," he added.

According to foreign news reports, Israel has a nuclear arsenal of at least 200 bombs. Israel declines comment on the issue, saying only that it would not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons to the Middle East.

Mubarak and Assad said they were not optimistic about a resumption in the near future of the stalled peace process and Mubarak said even the United States, which sponsors the peace process, was having problems with boosting the process.

"We are all wondering how to move the peace process forward before it becomes buried...We can see that there are problems between the U.S. and Israel in this issue but we are giving it time in the hope that the U.S. can achieve something with Israel," Mubarak said.

"We are trying to help from our side by doing what we can by exchanging views with the U.S. so that Israel can at least understand that peace, stability, cooperation have a price -- the return of (Arab) land," he added.
Assad, whose country has not held peace talks with Israel since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power in June, said "the doors of peace are closed".

"Under present circumstances, no one can determine, with confidence or positively, if there will be peace or not. There is nothing that can convince any Arab or non-Arab citizen that the doors of peace are open," Assad said.
"Neither the statements nor the actions of the Israeli government indicate that their direction is that of peace. Until now, my opinion is that the doors of peace are closed," he said.
Israel has held sporadic peace talks with Syria since 1991 but the negotiations were blocked over the fate of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War.
Mubarak said reports of an Arab summit on the stalled peace process were unwarranted.
Assad returned to Damascus after having lunch with Mubarak.
